statement: In a given pentagon, which is equilateral and equiangular, to inscribe a circle.
heath_proof: Let ABCDE be the given equilateral and equiangular pentagon; thus it is required to inscribe a circle in the pentagon ABCDE. For let the angles BCD, CDE be bisected by the straight lines CF, DF respectively; and from the point F, at which the straight lines CF, DF meet one another, let the straight lines FB, FA, FE be joined. Then, since BC is equal to CD, and CF common, the two sides BC, CF are equal to the two sides DC, CF; and the angle BCF is equal to the angle DCF; therefore the base BF is equal to the base DF, and the triangle BCF is equal to the triangle DCF, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles, namely those which the equal sides subtend. [I. 4] Therefore the angle CBF is equal to the angle CDF. And, since the angle CDE is double of the angle CDF, and the angle CDE is equal to the angle ABC, while the angle CDF is equal to the angle CBF; therefore the angle CBA is also double of the angle CBF; therefore the angle ABF is equal to the angle FBC; therefore the angle ABC has been bisected by the straight line BF. Similarly it can be proved that the angles BAE, AED have also been bisected by the straight lines FA, FE respectively. Now let FG, FH, FK, FL, FM be drawn from the point F perpendicular to the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA. Then, since the angle HCF is equal to the angle KCF, and the right angle FHC is also equal to the angle FKC, FHC, FKC are two triangles having two angles equal to two angles and one side equal to one side, namely FC which is common to them and subtends one of the equal angles; therefore they will also have the remaining sides equal to the remaining sides; [I. 26] therefore the perpendicular FH is equal to the perpendicular FK. Similarly it can be proved that each of the straight lines FL, FM, FG is also equal to each of the straight lines FH, FK; therefore the five straight lines FG, FH, FK, FL, FM are equal to one another. Therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FG, FH, FK, FL, FM will pass also through the remaining points; and it will touch the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA, because the angles at the points G, H, K, L, M are right. For, if it does not touch them. but cuts them, it will result that the straight line drawn at right angles to the diameter of the circle from its extremity falls within the circle: which was proved absurd. [III. 16] Therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FG, FH, FK, FL, FM will not cut the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA; therefore it will touch them. Let it be described, as GHKLM. Therefore in the given pentagon, which is equilateral and equiangular, a circle has been inscribed.

**Statement:** In a given pentagon, which is equilateral and equiangular, to inscribe a circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the given pentagon, equilateral and equiangular. Bisect the angle BCD by the straight line CF and the angle CDE by the straight line DF [1.9].

**Step 2.** The straight lines CF, DF meet. For the angle FCD is half of the angle BCD and the angle FDC is half of the angle CDE; each of the rectilineal angles BCD, CDE is less than two right angles, so each of the halves FCD, FDC is less than one right angle, and the interior angles FCD, FDC on the same side of CD are together less than two right angles. Hence CF, DF, being produced, meet on that side [P5]; let them meet at the point F. Join FB, FA, FE [P1].

**Step 3.** In the triangles BCF, DCF, the side BC is equal to the side DC (the pentagon is equilateral), CF is common, and the angle BCF is equal to the angle DCF (Step 1). Therefore the base BF is equal to the base DF, and the angle CBF is equal to the angle CDF [1.4].

**Step 4.** The angle CDE is the sum of the angles CDF, FDE, and these are equal (Step 1); so the angle CDE is double of the angle CDF. But the angle ABC is equal to the angle CDE (the pentagon is equiangular), and the angle CDF is equal to the angle CBF (Step 3); therefore the angle ABC is double of the angle CBF, that is, the angles ABF, FBC together are equal to the angles CBF, CBF together. Subtracting the common angle FBC, the remaining angle ABF is equal to the remaining angle FBC [CN3]. Therefore the angle ABC is bisected by BF.

**Step 5.** In the triangles ABF, CBF, the side AB is equal to the side CB, BF is common, and the angle ABF is equal to the angle CBF (Step 4). Therefore AF is equal to CF and the angle BAF is equal to the angle BCF [1.4]. Now the angle BCD is double of the angle BCF (Step 1), hence double of the angle BAF; and the angle BAE is equal to the angle BCD (equiangular), so the angle BAE is double of the angle BAF, and subtracting the common angle BAF, the angle EAF is equal to the angle BAF [CN3]. Therefore the angle BAE is bisected by AF.

**Step 6.** In the same manner, in the triangles CDF, EDF, the side CD is equal to the side ED, DF is common, and the angle CDF is equal to the angle EDF (Step 1); therefore CF is equal to EF and the angle DCF is equal to the angle DEF [1.4]. The angle BCD is double of the angle DCF, hence double of the angle DEF; and the angle DEA is equal to the angle BCD, so the angle DEA is double of the angle DEF, and subtracting the common angle DEF, the angle AEF is equal to the angle DEF [CN3]. Therefore the angle AED is bisected by EF. Thus each of the five angles of the pentagon is bisected by the straight line joining its vertex to F.

**Step 7.** From the point F draw FG, FH, FK, FL, FM perpendicular to the straight lines AB, BC, CD, DE, EA respectively [1.12]. Then the angles at G, H, K, L, M are right angles [D1.10].

**Step 8.** In the triangles FHC, FKC, the angle HCF is equal to the angle KCF (Step 1), the angle FHC is equal to the angle FKC, both being right [P4], and the side FC is common, subtending one of the equal angles in each. Therefore the remaining sides are equal, so that FH is equal to FK [1.26]. Similarly, from the triangles FKD, FLD (the angle KDF being equal to the angle LDF by Step 1) FK is equal to FL; from the triangles FLE, FME (the angle LEF being equal to the angle MEF by Step 6) FL is equal to FM; and from the triangles FMA, FGA (the angle MAF being equal to the angle GAF by Step 5) FM is equal to FG. Therefore the five straight lines FG, FH, FK, FL, FM are equal to one another [CN1].

**Step 9.** With centre F and distance FG let the circle GHKLM be described [P3]. Since FH, FK, FL, FM are each equal to FG, the circle described with centre F and distance FG passes also through the points H, K, L, M [D1.15].

**Step 10.** The straight line AB is drawn through the extremity G of the radius FG at right angles to FG, that is, at right angles to the diameter of the circle through G. If AB cut the circle, a straight line drawn at right angles to a diameter from its extremity would fall within the circle, which is impossible [3.16]; hence AB meets the circle at G only and does not cut it, so AB touches the circle [D3.2]. In the same way, since the angles at H, K, L, M are right, each of BC, CD, DE, EA touches the circle GHKLM at H, K, L, M respectively [3.16, D3.2].

**Step 11.** Therefore the circumference of the circle GHKLM touches each of the sides AB, BC, CD, DE, EA of the pentagon; that is, the circle GHKLM is inscribed in the given equilateral and equiangular pentagon ABCDE [D4.5]. Q.E.F.
